match.reason: The bank point teaches the same idea that profit can rise before cash arrives, its terms and examples suit Victorian Accounting, and both questions are fair, though its depth is set for Units 1 and 2 rather than Units 3 and 4.

confirm.reason: The bank card acc-cash-profit teaches the same idea at Units 1 and 2 depth and covers only revenue timing, while this Year 12 point also needs expense timing (such as prepaid and accrued expenses and depreciation) and the link between the Income Statement and the Cash Flow Statement, which is a deeper treatment.

draft.title: Cash and profit compared
card: revenue less expenses. Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash has moved.
the money actually received and paid in the period. The cash flow statement reports it.
The two differ because of timing. A credit sale adds revenue now but brings in cash later. Buying inventory uses cash, but inventory is not an expense until it is sold.
Depreciation is an expense that uses no cash in the period. So a business can report a profit and still have too little cash to pay its bills on time.
draft.remember: Profit follows when revenue and expenses are recorded. Cash follows when money moves.

a.q: Why can a business report a profit for the year and still run short of cash?
opts: Revenue is recorded when earned, but cash may arrive later
Profit is worked out from cash received, so it matches cash
Expenses are recorded only when they are paid in cash
Profit is always paid out to the owner as drawings
a.why: Under accrual accounting, a credit sale is revenue now, but the cash comes in later. Profit is not worked out from cash received, so it can be well above the cash on hand.
a.clue: Think about a sale made on credit.

b.q: Priya's Cycles in Ballarat made a profit this year. It sold many bikes on credit, and it also bought a large amount of inventory that is still unsold. Which statement best explains why its bank balance fell?
opts: Credit sales are not yet cash, and unsold stock used cash
Credit sales are not yet cash, and unsold stock is an expense
Credit sales cut profit, and unsold stock used cash
Credit sales are not revenue, and unsold stock is an expense
b.why: Credit sales are recorded as revenue, so profit rises, but the cash has not arrived. Buying inventory pays out cash, yet it is not an expense until the bikes are sold. The tempting option treats unsold stock as an expense, which would also lower profit.
b.clue: Is inventory an expense before it is sold?
